transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ___. What brings you in today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doc. Uh, the thing is... I've been working as a customer service rep for a good long while now, and, well, I guess what brings me in is that I just feel like I’m always moving from one thing to the next. I really can’t just idle. It’s like, I don't know, like a car engine that's just left running all the time. 

Even when I'm on the phone with a customer, I’m shifting around, I'm standing up, I'm pacing as far as the headset cord lets me, I'm looking for a pen that I don't even need... I just can't just sit there and do nothing. And, you know, for years it was fine. I had my own little high-walled cubicle and nobody really bothered me as long as my call times were good and the customers were happy. 

But recently, the company completely changed our office around. We've got this new work setup now—they knocked down all the dividers, put us in these open little pods, and the supervisors are right there, practically breathing down our necks all day. And, honestly, this new setup has made it a lot harder to hide the fact that I'm constantly in motion. My boss keeps giving me these looks when I stand up for the fifth time in an hour, and it's just... it's getting exhausting trying to force myself to stay glued to that chair. I come home totally wiped out just from trying to sit still. So, I figured I had better come in and talk to somebody about it.
Do you also have trouble keeping your attention on tasks?

Well, yeah, actually. It's funny you bring that up because with all the changes at the office lately, they've been pulling us into these longer coaching meetings. You know, they want to go over the new metrics, how we're supposed to handle the call flow now, all the new corporate policies. And they're always handing us these thick printouts of new procedures to read through. 

And I really try to focus on it, I do. I sit there and I start off just fine. I'm looking right at the paper, thinking, alright, let's get this down, let's learn the new rules. But then... well, it's like, after just a few minutes, I'll suddenly snap to and realize that my eyes have just been moving down the page, line by line, doing all the physical work of reading, but I didn't actually take in a single word. Or if it's one of those long meetings, I'll be staring right at the manager while they talk, nodding along, and then I realize my mind went completely blank and I have no earthly idea what was just said. 

It's like the words just turn into background noise after a little while. Then I have to go all the way back to the top of the page and start reading all over again, and by then I'm worried someone's gonna notice I'm falling behind the rest of the group. It just takes so much effort to keep my brain locked onto the actual task when it's something long like that, you know? It's really frustrating, especially now that everyone can see me at my desk.
Were you having these kinds of attention and restlessness problems as a child?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because when all this started happening with the new office layout and everything, I actually found myself thinking back to when I was a kid. And, well, yeah, honestly, this whole thing—the restlessness, the trouble focusing—it’s been around for a long, long time. Way before this job change, way before I even started working at this company, to be perfectly honest. 

I remember, clear as day, being back in grade school. You know, back then they didn't really have all these names for things like they do now, but I remember my mom keeping all my old report cards in this big manila envelope in the hall closet. And every single year, it seemed like, the teachers would write the exact same kind of comments. They’d always say, "He's a bright boy, very capable," but then right after that, there was always a "but." It was always, "but he's careless," or "he rushes through his assignments and makes silly mistakes." 

And the talking! Oh boy, I was always getting in trouble for talking out of turn. I just couldn't seem to hold a thought in—if it popped into my head, it came right out of my mouth before I even realized I was speaking. I’d be blurting out answers before the teacher even finished the question, or I’d be turning around in my desk to talk to the kid behind me while we were supposed to be doing silent reading. 

And they were constantly having to remind me to just stay with my work. I’d start a math worksheet, do the first three problems, and then suddenly I’m staring out the window watching the janitor mow the lawn, or I’m taking my pen apart to see how the spring works. The teacher would have to walk by and tap on my desk, like, "Earth to him, let's get back to the fractions." So, yeah, looking back on it now, it’s like... it’s always been there, just kind of humming in the background my whole life, you know? It just wasn't causing me this much grief until they knocked down those cubicle walls.
Do you find yourself avoiding social situations mainly because you’re worried other people will judge or criticize you?

No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I don't really shy away from being around people or anything like that. It's not like I'm sitting at home worrying that someone's going to look at me funny or, you know, judge me for what I'm wearing or what I say. Actually, I've always been pretty comfortable talking to folks—I mean, I've been in customer service for, gosh, almost thirty years now, so you kind of have to be, right? You get all sorts on the phone, the angry ones, the confused ones, the ones who just want to chat your ear off about their grandkids when all you're trying to do is reset their password. You learn real quick not to take things personally or worry too much about what strangers think of you.

So, socially, no, I don't avoid things out of fear of criticism. If I go to a neighborhood barbecue or the company holiday party—well, back when they used to throw a decent holiday party, before they started just handing out five-dollar coffee gift cards and calling it a day—I'm usually right in the mix. I'm the guy by the snack table, talking to whoever comes up. The only issue I ever really run into socially is that, well, like I was saying before, I just can't always sit still for it. Like if someone invites me to go see a long movie, or sit through a three-hour dinner at a fancy restaurant where you're just trapped at the table waiting for the next course... that's the kind of thing I might try to wiggle out of. Not because I'm worried they're judging me, but just because the thought of being stuck in one chair for that long makes my skin crawl. But just hanging out and talking? No, that doesn't bother me a bit. I don't really care what people think in that regard, as long as I can keep my feet moving a little.
